title: When to Accept Differences in Views and When to Stand Your Ground
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes between decisions where leaders should willingly defer to their team and decisions where they must hold firm. On tactics, solutions to smaller problems, and matters within team members' expertise, good leaders intentionally let others win, building ownership and engagement. But when it comes to an organization's core vision, mission, and values, the piece argues leaders cannot simply defer to consensus without undermining the clarity the team needs to function. It closes by warning that winning every argument can cost a leader the team's engagement, while giving away the organization's values costs something far more fundamental.
points: Good leaders intentionally lose some arguments and defer to team expertise on many decisions.
Letting the team win on tactics and smaller solutions builds pride and ownership.
Leaders must hold firm on the organization's core vision, mission, and values.
Deferring on core values, even to build goodwill, undermines the clarity the team needs.
Knowing which battles to concede and which to defend is described as a defining leadership skill.
quotes: Good leaders make it a point to occasionally lose arguments, to be outvoted by the team, and to concede to the wisdom of others whenever they can.
Leaders who “get it” defer to the subject-matter expertise of those team members who are true experts on the issues at hand.
But good leaders stand their ground when it comes to the vision, mission, and values of the organization or team.
Leaders who mistakenly allow the team to have an undue influence over the vision and values of the organization relinquish their role as the leader.
The best leaders concede that they don’t have to have their way on many of the decisions critical for executing strategy.
Sometimes, winning the argument is how to lose the team. But the vision, mission, and values of the team are never up for grabs.
